# TypeScript AI Framework for Agents and Apps

Ship AI agents that reason, remember, and act in TypeScript. Mastra provides memory, tools, MCP, and observability to go from prototype to production.

Build agents that do the work, not just answer questions. Mastra is an open-source TypeScript framework for agents and workflows: connect models to your tools and data, give agents memory, and keep people involved when a task needs judgment.

Start with a single agent. Add workflows for steps that need a defined sequence, a harness for long-running work, and evals to measure whether your changes make the agent better.

Create a project:

```sh
npm create mastra@latest
```

Follow the [documentation](https://mastra.ai/docs.md) to configure your first agent. If you're a local coding agent with filesystem access, install the skills to get up-to-date guidance:

```sh
npx skills add mastra-ai/skills
```

## Agent framework

- **Agents**: choose a model, write instructions, and connect tools so your agent can act on your systems, not just generate text. [Agent documentation](https://mastra.ai/docs/agents/overview.md)
- **Workflows**: define typed steps, branches, and retries for processes that need predictable control flow. Pause for human input and resume when a decision is made. [Workflow documentation](https://mastra.ai/docs/workflows/overview.md)
- **Harness**: manage long-running work with persistent sessions, plan-and-build modes, tool approvals, and subagents. Send updates through Signals while an agent works. These are the primitives behind Mastra Code.
- **Memory**: retain useful context across conversations with observational memory, semantic recall, and thread storage. [Memory documentation](https://mastra.ai/docs/memory/overview.md)
- **Server**: expose agents and workflows through API endpoints. Develop locally, then deploy on your own infrastructure or Mastra Platform.
- **Factory**: coordinate coding agents from issue investigation through implementation and pull request review, with checkpoints for your team. [Mastra Factory](https://mastra.ai/factory)

## Observability

See what happened in a run, then test whether a change fixes it. Mastra pairs observability with evals and datasets so you can move from debugging individual failures to checking behavior across repeatable test cases.

- **Evals**: score agent output and behavior with code-based checks or model-based judges. Compare changes before shipping them. [Evals documentation](https://mastra.ai/docs/evals/overview.md)
- **Metrics**: track latency, token usage, and cost to understand where time and money go.
- **Datasets**: turn real inputs and expected outputs into versioned test cases. Run experiments to compare models, prompts, and agent configurations.
- **Tracing**: follow model calls, tool calls, and workflow steps to see where a run went wrong. [Tracing documentation](https://mastra.ai/docs/observability/tracing/overview.md)

[Observability documentation](https://mastra.ai/docs/observability/overview.md)

## Use cases

Build agents for your customers, your team, or your development process. Connect the tools and data each job requires, and decide which actions need human approval.

- **Customer support**: answer product questions from your documentation, investigate account issues, and prepare actions for a support team to approve.
- **Company knowledge**: search internal documents and connected data sources, then answer questions with references to the evidence.
- **Research assistants**: investigate a topic, compare sources, follow up on gaps, and produce a report others can verify.
- **Data analysis**: turn questions into database queries, analyze CSV files, and summarize the results.
- **Document processing**: extract structured data from PDFs and invoices, check it against existing records, and flag exceptions for review.
- **Coding agents**: investigate issues, plan changes, edit code, run tests, and review pull requests.
- **Incident response**: gather logs and deployment context, investigate likely causes, and propose next steps for an engineer to approve.
- **Customer feedback analysis**: find recurring problems across support conversations and customer feedback, then turn them into a product brief.
- **Team assistants**: bring work into Slack or other messaging channels, prepare daily briefings, and follow up on unfinished tasks.

Every documentation page is available as markdown. The index is at [`/llms.txt`](https://mastra.ai/llms.txt).

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Mastra?

Mastra is an open-source TypeScript framework for building AI-powered applications and agents. Mastra provides agents, workflows, memory, workspaces and observability, letting developers go from idea to implementation. Mastra integrates with frontend and backend frameworks like React, Next.js and Node, or can be deployed anywhere as a standalone server.

### Is Mastra an agent builder?

Mastra is a TypeScript framework for building AI agents and AI-powered applications. Mastra agents use LLMs and tools to solve open-ended tasks, reasoning about goals, deciding which tools to use and iterating internally until the model emits a final answer or an optional stopping condition is met. Mastra also provides workflows, memory, workspaces and observability to support the full agent development lifecycle.

### What can you build with Mastra?

Mastra supports building AI-powered applications that combine language understanding, reasoning and action to solve real-world tasks. Mastra use cases include conversational agents for customer support, onboarding or internal queries, domain-specific copilots for coding, legal, finance, research or creative work, workflow automations that trigger, route and complete multi-step processes, and decision-support tools that analyze data and provide actionable recommendations.

### What AI models and providers does Mastra support?

Mastra's model routing connects to 90+ providers through one standard interface. Mastra supports models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and more, allowing developers to use different AI providers through a single API.

### What are Mastra workflows?

Mastra's graph-based workflow engine orchestrates complex multi-step processes with explicit control over execution. Mastra workflows use an intuitive syntax for control flow including .then(), .branch() and .parallel() methods. Mastra workflows also support human-in-the-loop functionality, allowing developers to suspend a workflow and await user input or approval before resuming. Mastra uses storage to remember execution state, so workflows can pause indefinitely and resume where they left off.

### How does Mastra handle agent memory and context?

Mastra's memory system provides conversation history, data retrieval from APIs, databases and files, and human-like working and semantic memory so agents behave coherently. Developers can give Mastra agents the right context at the right time by combining message history with retrieval from external data sources.

### Does Mastra support MCP servers?

Mastra supports authoring Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, exposing agents, tools and other structured resources via the MCP interface. MCP servers built with Mastra can be accessed by any system or agent that supports the protocol.

### How does Mastra handle testing and observability?

Mastra includes built-in scorers and observability tools to observe, measure and refine agent performance continuously. Mastra supports evaluating agent output using model-graded, rule-based and statistical methods, with custom evals to track agent performance over time. Mastra's observability features trace agent calls and token usage with support for external observability platforms. Mastra also provides guardrails to process inputs and outputs, helping prevent prompt injection and sanitize responses.

### How do you deploy Mastra applications?

Mastra applications can be deployed to any Node.js-compatible environment. Mastra includes optional built-in deployers for Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare to automate the deployment process. Developers can also deploy Mastra as a standalone server powered by Hono, integrate it with existing web frameworks like Next.js, or use their existing Hono, Express, Fastify or any other server app.

### Why use Mastra instead of a Python AI framework?

Mastra is purpose-built for TypeScript and designed around established AI patterns, giving TypeScript developers everything they need to build AI applications out of the box. Mastra bundles agents and workflows directly into existing React, Next.js and Node.js apps, or ships them as standalone endpoints. Mastra provides a complete set of AI primitives including workflows, agents, workspaces and observability in one modular framework.

### Is Mastra open source?

Mastra's core framework is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Enterprise features are source-available under the Mastra Enterprise License. Mastra is free to start with no seats or usage tiers.

## Plan Feature Details

**Throughput** is the guaranteed number of successful searches per hour for your plan. To improve performance, distribute your searches evenly throughout the hour and across multiple hours.

**U.S. Legal Shield** provides up to $2 million in coverage for the scraping and parsing of search engine data, as long as your use of the data or service is not illegal.

**ZeroTrace Mode** prevents search data from being stored on our systems. When enabled, we do not retain search parameters, queries, or results, and each request is discarded after completion, reducing traceability and supporting privacy and compliance requirements.

**Priority Support** gives you faster response times and dedicated assistance from our support team.

## Speed Modes

Every plan can be combined with a speed mode. Speed modes use additional server resources to deliver faster, more consistent response times.

| Mode | Price Multiplier | Details |
|------|------------------|---------|
| Best Effort | 1× base price | Default mode included with every plan at no extra cost. |
| Ludicrous Speed | 2× base price | Uses 2× the server resources for significantly faster response times. Delivers 2.2× faster average response times and 4.2× faster p99 compared to Best Effort. |
| Ludicrous Speed Max | 4× base price | Uses 4× the server resources for maximum speed and consistency. Delivers 9.6% faster average response times and 35.4% faster p99 compared to Ludicrous Speed. |

## Need more volume?

Contact us at **contact@serpapi.com**. We'll be glad to help.

## FAQs

### How are searches counted?

Only successful searches are counted toward your monthly searches. Cached, errored, and failed searches are not. The number of results returned per response will not affect the number of credits used—responses with 100 results or empty result sets will both count as 1 search.

### Can we upgrade, downgrade, or cancel at any time?

Yes, you can upgrade, downgrade, or cancel your plan at any time without any restrictions.

### What happens if I cancel before my plan expires?

If you cancel before your plan expires, you can continue to use your remaining searches until the renewal date. After that, your plan will not be renewed.

### What happens when I upgrade my plan?

When you upgrade your plan, you'll only pay the difference between your current plan and the new one. Your renewal date will remain the same.

### What happens when I downgrade my plan?

When you downgrade your plan, you'll keep your current renewal date, and your subscription will renew at the lower plan rate. Any remaining searches from your previous plan will be added to your 'Extra Credits' balance.

### What happens if I run out of searches in a month?

You can set your plan to Automatic Early Renewal. It will trigger an early renewal once you've used all your searches. You can toggle the Automatic Early Renewal anytime by visiting [this page](https://serpapi.com/plan). You can also renew your plan manually. In both cases, your searches will be fully replenished, your renewal date will be updated, and your searches will reset at the start of the new billing cycle.

### What's your refund policy?

We offer a full refund within 7 days of the date you subscribed to a plan unless you've used more than 20% of your searches.

What is a .tech domain, and who is it for?

.tech is a Top-Level Domain (nTLD) for tech startups. It tells VCs, customers, and the world that your startup’s core is tech.

How do I get a .tech domain?

You can get it right here. Just scroll up and search for the domain you want in the search bar. Prefer a registrar? .tech is available on GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare, Domain.com, 1&1 Ionos, OVHCloud, and Network Solutions.

What’s Privacy Protection and do I need it?

When you register a domain, your contact information, like name, email, and registered address, shows up in the public WHOIS directory by default. Privacy Protection hides that and replaces it with generic details so your data stays private.

How do I purchase, enable or disable Privacy Protection?

If Privacy Protection is not included with your domain, you can purchase it during registration or later through your .tech or registrar control panel.

To enable or disable Privacy Protection, follow these steps:

- Log in to the .tech [control panel](http://manage.get.tech/customer) (visit the registrar website if you haven’t purchased through .tech)

- Go to your domain settings

- Find the Privacy Protection or WHOIS Privacy option

- Turn it on or off

- Save your changes

Does .tech offer hosting?

No, we don’t offer hosting.

How do I manage my domain name(s)?

To manage your domain name(s), log in to the .tech [control panel](http://manage.get.tech/customer) using the email ID and password you registered with. For step-by-step instructions, refer to [this guide](https://manage.get.tech/kb/servlet/KBServlet/cat119.html). If you bought your .tech domain from a registrar, check their website for information on how to manage your domain name(s) through their portal.

I got my .tech domain. What else do I need to set up a website?

Once you’ve got your .tech domain, connect it to your website by updating the name servers or A record with your hosting provider. You can do this through the .tech control panel or the control panel of the registrar you bought your domain from.

How do I add the name servers or A Records to the domain name?

If you bought your .tech domain directly from us, follow these steps:

- Log in to the .tech [control panel](http://manage.get.tech/customer)

- Search for your domain and go to the Order Information view

- Click on the Name Servers link

- Add up to 13 name servers and click Update

- If you bought your domain through a registrar, visit their website for steps on adding name servers or A records.

How can I set up a redirect?

You can redirect your website using the Domain Forwarding service.

To set up Domain Forwarding, follow these steps:

- Log in to the .tech [control panel](http://manage.get.tech/customer) and select your .tech domain

- Go to the Domain Forwarding section and click Manage Domain Forwarding

- Enter the destination URL and click Save

I have purchased a domain that I no longer require. How can I cancel my domain and get a refund?

Deleting a domain is permanent. It can’t be undone, and there are no refunds for the domain or any services linked to it.

To delete your domain, follow these steps:

- Log in to the .tech [control panel](http://manage.get.tech/customer), search for the domain, and open the Order Details view

- Click the Delete Order link

- Confirm the deletion on the next page

- Once you delete your domain, any connected websites, email accounts, or services will stop working and can’t be recovered.

I accidentally deleted my domain. How can I restore it?

Unfortunately, deleted domains can’t be restored. Deletion is permanent, and the domain is immediately lost. You can try registering the domain again, but note that availability is not guaranteed.

What happens if I forget to renew my domain and it expires?

If your .tech domain expires, here's what happens:

- Days 1-36: Renewal Grace Period

  Your domain stops working, but you can still renew it at the regular price.

- Days 37-66: Redemption Period

  You can restore your domain by paying a restoration fee and the renewal cost.

- Days 67-71: Pending Delete

  The domain is locked. You can’t renew or recover it.

- After Day 71: Publicly Available

  The domain is deleted and open for anyone to register. Popular domains may get snapped up instantly.

Best move? Renew early or for multiple years. It’s the easiest way to avoid losing your domain.

What do I do if I forget to renew my domain?

We send multiple reminders before your domain expires. Mandatory emails go out 30 and 7 days before expiry. You can also choose to get reminders on the 1st, 11th, and 21st day in the last 45 days. These can be managed from your .tech or registrar control panel.

If you miss the deadline, you have a 36-day Grace Period to renew your domain at the regular price. After that, your domain enters a 30-day Redemption Period. You can recover it, but the process includes a restoration fee.

For more information, refer to [this guide](https://manage.get.tech/kb/servlet/KBServlet/faq460.html).

Can I transfer my domain to another provider or registrar?

Yes, you can transfer your domain to another provider or registrar. Transfer charges apply. Before you begin, check that your domain is eligible. For detailed steps and eligibility checks, refer to [this guide](https://manage.get.tech/kb/servlet/KBServlet/faq556.html).

What’s a Premium domain? What’s a Reserved domain? Why do they cost more?

Premium domains are short, easy to remember, and often include popular keywords. They're priced higher—at varying costs—based on factors like character count, search demand, recall value, and potential to drive traffic.

Reserved domains are held back by the registry. This could be due to policy restrictions, sensitive terms, or internal use. These domain names may not be available for registration.

Want to check domain availability? Reach out to our support team at [support@get.tech](mailto:support@get.tech)

Who do I report abuse to?

To report abuse related to a .tech domain, fill out [this form](https://abuse.radix.website/).

Who do I contact for support?

For any support-related queries, send an email to [support@get.tech](mailto:support@get.tech)

Atlas SQL Interface (Dedicated Cluster) is billed as a simple daily uplift based on your cluster tier size and on your cluster spend, not a per query bill.

## FAQ

### Is there a free tier available for MongoDB Atlas? What does it include?

Yes, MongoDB Atlas offers a free-forever tier, the M0. Atlas’s free tier includes 512 MB of storage, 32MB of sort memory, and up to 100 operations per second. The free tier is a great starting point to learn about MongoDB and explore its capabilities in a fully managed cloud environment.

[Get started with a free tier →](https://www.mongodb.com/cloud/atlas/register)  
[Atlas Free tier features and limitations →](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/)  
[Guide: How to deploy a free tier cluster →](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/tutorial/deploy-free-tier-cluster/)

### How do I choose the right cluster tier for my application?

Choosing the right MongoDB Atlas cluster tier for your application involves considering the application's workload, data size, and performance needs. Key considerations include:

- **Free Tier (M0):** Best for learning and exploring, with [limited resources](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/).

- **Flex:** Ideal for development and testing, offering the lowest cost option with certain [feature limitations](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/flex-limitations/#std-label-atlas-flex-limitations).

- **Dedicated (M10 & M20):** Suitable for pre-production and small, non-critical workloads. These tiers utilize shared vCPUs and support replica set deployments offering fully featured access to Atlas.

- **Dedicated (M30+):** Recommended for performance-critical and high-traffic workloads, supporting both replica sets and sharded clusters with fully featured access to Atlas with dedicated vCPUs.

Clusters can always be scaled up from any tier as requirements expand. If unsure, MongoDB recommends starting with a lower tier and [monitoring performance](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/monitoring-alerts/) before adjusting. For all Dedicated tiers, use auto-scaling to adjust cluster tier and storage as workloads evolve.

[How to select your cluster tier →](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/manage-clusters/#select-cluster-tier)  
[Atlas cluster sizing and tier selection →](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/sizing-tier-selection/)  
[Learn more about dedicated clusters →](https://www.mongodb.com/products/platform/dedicated-clusters)

### What factors influence my MongoDB Atlas costs?

MongoDB Atlas costs are based on a pay-as-you-go model, influenced by several key factors:

- **Cluster tier and type:** The selected tier is the foundational cost driver. Higher tiers provide more dedicated resources and capabilities.

- **Cloud provider and region:** Costs vary slightly across AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, and between different geographic regions.

- **Data storage:** Includes the size of your data and indexes.

- **Data transfer (networking):** Charges mainly apply to data moving out of your Atlas cluster (egress) or between different regions/cloud providers. Inbound data transfers are typically free. Free and Flex tiers are not charged for outgoing data.

- **Backup services:** Costs are based on the region and the monthly storage consumed by snapshots and oplogs for continuous backups. Note that backup services are not available for the Free tier.

- **Add-on tools and services:** Additional add-on tools and services contribute to the overall cost. Examples include but are not limited to:

  - Atlas Stream Processing

  - Dedicated MongoDB Search on Atlas Nodes

  - Support subscriptions

  - Premium Atlas Charts features

Additional factors that can influence cost over time include:

- Fluctuations in usage

- Configuration adjustments

- Auto-scaling behavior

- New features

- Cloud provider price changes

[Atlas cluster configuration costs →](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/cluster-configuration-costs/)  
[Understand Your MongoDB Invoice →](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/invoice-breakdown/#std-label-atlas-invoice-breakdown)

### How do I manage and reduce MongoDB Atlas costs?

**Right-size clusters:** Pause development or testing clusters when not in use. Alternatively, terminate them if no longer required. For Dedicated clusters, use [auto-scaling](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/cluster-autoscaling/) to adjust cluster storage and/or tier based on real-time CPU and memory utilization.

**Optimize data management:** Design efficient [schemas](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/schema-design-process/) and use strategic [indexing](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/indexes/) to improve query performance while minimizing resource consumption. Regularly review clusters, databases, and collections to eliminate duplication, outdated data, and unused sample datasets. For Dedicated clusters, use Atlas [Online Archive](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/online-archive/manage-online-archive/) to tier infrequently accessed data, which will reduce primary storage costs.

**Minimize data transfer:** Reduce [data transfer costs](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/) by heeding the following best practices:

- Avoid queries that re-read client data or re-write existing cluster data.

- Use query projections to only retrieve necessary fields.

- Deploy applications in the same cloud region as the Atlas cluster.

- Enable network compression in client drivers to reduce data volume.

**Monitor & alerts:** Regularly review spending patterns using the [Billing Cost Explorer](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/#billing-cost-explorer) tool in Atlas. Additionally, set up billing [alerts](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/monitoring-alerts/#std-label-arch-center-monitoring-alerts-recs) to be notified of unexpected cost spikes or when usage approaches predefined thresholds.

[Billing breakdown and optimization →](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/billing-breakdown-optimization/)

## Introduction

Temporal is a durable execution platform that enables developers to build scalable applications without sacrificing productivity or reliability.
The Temporal server executes units of application logic called Workflows in a resilient manner that automatically handles intermittent failures, and retries failed operations.

Temporal is a mature technology that originated as a fork of Uber's Cadence.
It is developed by Temporal Technologies, a startup by the creators of Cadence.

...

## Getting Started

### Download and Start Temporal Server Locally

Execute the following commands to start a pre-built image along with all the dependencies.

```bash
brew install temporal
temporal server start-dev
```

Refer to Temporal CLI documentation for more installation options.

### Run the Samples

Clone or download samples for Go or Java and run them with the local Temporal server.
We have a number of HelloWorld type scenarios available, as well as more advanced ones. Note that the sets of samples are currently different between Go and Java.

### Use CLI

Use Temporal CLI to interact with the running Temporal server.

```bash
temporal operator namespace list
temporal workflow list
```

### Use Temporal Web UI

Try Temporal Web UI by opening http://localhost:8233 for viewing your sample workflows executing on Temporal.

## Repository

This repository contains the source code of the Temporal server. To implement Workflows, Activities and Workers, use one of the supported languages.

development server is designed to handle. For local development or testing, you can use the
Temporal CLI to start a local development Temporal Service.

> ⚠️ Warning:
> Temporal Hosts Should Not Be Exposed to the Open Internet
> 
> In self-hosted deployments, the Temporal Service is a critical control and persistence component and should be secured
> similarly to a database. Temporal services should run on hosts that are not accessible from the public internet, with
> network configurations that restrict access to trusted internal networks only.

For step-by-step guides on deploying and configuring Temporal, refer to our
Infrastructure tutorials.

## Use Docker Compose

You can run a Temporal Service in Docker containers using
Docker Compose.

### Prerequisites

- You have Docker Compose installed.
- Docker is running and the daemon is available.
- Git is installed and available.

### Procedure

1. Clone the temporalio/samples-server repository. The docker-compose.yml example uses the `temporalio/server:${TEMPORAL_VERSION}` image. This is what you need to use in your production environments and you can find a thorough list of configs here.
2. Change into the `compose` directory.

```
cd samples-server/compose

```

1. Run the `docker compose up` command. This uses the default configuration from the `docker-compose.yaml` file, which
includes a PostgreSQL database, an Elasticsearch instance, and exposes the Temporal gRPC Frontend on port 7233.

```
docker compose up

```

The Temporal Web UI will be available at `http://localhost:8080`.

1. (Optional) Review
the additional configuration options
available in the samples-server repository and use `docker compose up` with the corresponding configuration file to
try them out. The configurations include different databases, visibility stores, and TLS settings.

When you use the `temporalio/server` image, you have to manually manage schema updates using the `temporalio/admin-tools` image or by building the tools from the matching release tag.

## Use Temporal Server binaries

You can run a complete Temporal Server by deploying two Go binaries -- the
core Temporal Server, and the
Temporal UI Server.

Each service can be deployed separately. Refer to
How to Configure a Temporal Service without a Proxy
to deploy each service using `systemd`. If you need to run the Temporal Server behind a reverse proxy, refer to our
tutorials to deploy the Temporal Service behind an
Nginx reverse proxy or an
Envoy edge proxy.

...

The Temporal Server is a standalone Go application that can be imported into another
project.

You might want to do this to pass custom plugins or any other customizations through the
Server Options. Then you can build and run a binary that contains your customizations.

This requires the minimum Go version listed in the Temporal Server
`go.mod` file. See the Temporal Server
Build prerequisites.

## Use Helm charts

Temporal Helm charts enable you to get a Temporal Service running on
Kubernetes by deploying the Temporal Server services to individual pods and connecting them to
your existing database and Elasticsearch instances.

The Temporal Helm charts repo contains
extensive documentation about Kubernetes deployments.

## What is the Temporal Server?

The Temporal Server consists of four independently scalable services:

- Frontend gateway: for rate limiting, routing, authorizing.
- History subsystem: maintains data (mutable state, queues, and timers).
- Matching subsystem: hosts Task Queues for dispatching.
- Worker Service: for internal background Workflows.

For example, a real-life production deployment can have 5 Frontend, 15 History, 17 Matching, and 3 Worker Services per Temporal Service.

The Temporal Server services can run independently or be grouped together into shared processes on one or more physical or virtual machines.
For live (production) environments, we recommend that each service runs independently, because each one has different scaling requirements and troubleshooting becomes easier.
The History, Matching, and Worker Services can scale horizontally within a Temporal Service.
The Frontend Service scales differently than the others because it has no sharding or partitioning; it is just stateless.

### What Is Temporal?

Temporal is an open-source Durable Execution platform that allows developers to build applications that automatically survive failures, retries, network outages, and service crashes. Rather than writing complex retry logic, state machines, or reconciliation code, developers write ordinary business logic as Temporal Workflows, and the platform guarantees that execution will complete — even across infrastructure failures. Temporal is available as a self-hosted open-source project (MIT license) and as a fully managed service called Temporal Cloud.

### Is Temporal open source?

Yes. The core Temporal project is fully open source under the MIT license and available at https://github.com/temporalio/temporal. Temporal can be self-hosted in any environment. Temporal Cloud is the company's managed service offering, built on the same open-source foundation. Temporal never sees a customer's code or sensitive data in either deployment model.

Temporal Cloud is a fully managed service that hosts the Temporal Service on behalf of customers. With Temporal Cloud, teams do not need to manage, scale, upgrade, or operate the Temporal infrastructure or its underlying database — they only manage and deploy their own Workers and business logic. Temporal Cloud delivers 99.99% uptime, scales automatically to 300,000+ Actions/second, and is SOC 2 / GDPR / HIPAA compliant. ## Use Docker Compose

You can run a Temporal Service in Docker containers using

### Prerequisites

- You have Docker Compose installed.
- Docker is running and the daemon is available.

```

1. Run the `docker compose up` command. This uses the default configuration from the `docker-compose.yaml` file, which

```

```

The Temporal Web UI will be available at `http://localhost:8080`.

1. (Optional) Review

to deploy each service using `systemd`. If you need to run the Temporal Server behind a reverse proxy, refer to our
tutorials to deploy the Temporal Service behind an
Nginx reverse proxy or an

## What is the Temporal Server?

The Temporal Server consists of four independently scalable services:

- Frontend gateway: for rate limiting, routing, authorizing.
- History subsystem: maintains data (mutable state, queues, and timers).
- Matching subsystem: hosts Task Queues for dispatching.
- Worker Service: for internal background Workflows.

For example, a real-life production deployment can have 5 Frontend, 15 History, 17 Matching, and 3 Worker Services per Temporal Service.

The Temporal Server services can run independently or be grouped together into shared processes on one or more physical or virtual machines.
For live (production) environments, we recommend that each service runs independently, because each one has different scaling requirements and troubleshooting becomes easier.
The History, Matching, and Worker Services can scale horizontally within a Temporal Service.
The Frontend Service scales differently than the others because it has no sharding or partitioning; it is just stateless.

 * Facts in this file are intentionally structured rather than embedded in

 * Prices, quotas, and plan names change; the verification policy in
 * `docs/TOOL_CATALOG.md` defines when an entry must be re-checked.

export const TOOL_CATALOG_VERSION = "2026.10.31.1";
export const TOOL_CATALOG_VERIFIED_ON = "2026-10-31";
export const TOOL_CATALOG_STALE_AFTER_DAYS = 120;

  "public-deployment",
  "observability",
  "documentation",
  "ci",
  "code-history",
  "testing",
  "accessibility",
]);
export type ToolCategory = z.infer<typeof toolCategorySchema>;

export const opennessSchema = z.enum(["open-source", "open-weight", "proprietary", "mixed"]);
export type Openness = z.infer<typeof opennessSchema>;

export const costKindSchema = z.enum([
  "open-source",
  "open-weight",
  "self-hosted-free",
  "proprietary-free-tier",
  "trial",
  "paid-only",
  "hardware",
  "mixed",
]);
export type CostKind = z.infer<typeof costKindSchema>;

export const setupModeSchema = z.enum(["local", "hosted", "hybrid", "hardware"]);
export const effortSchema = z.enum(["low", "medium", "high"]);
export const toolStatusSchema = z.enum(["core", "conditional", "promo-only", "excluded"]);
export const recommendationRoleSchema = z.enum([
  "product-harness",
  "application",
  "observability",
  "build-history",
  "deployment",
  "utility",
]);

export const toolCostSchema = z.object({
  kind: costKindSchema,
  freeTier: z.boolean(),
  promotional: z.boolean(),
  permanentFree: z.boolean(),
  summary: z.string().min(1),
  limits: z.array(z.string().min(1)).min(1),
});

export const toolComponentSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1),
  openness: opennessSchema,
  license: z.string().min(1),
  costKind: costKindSchema,
  summary: z.string().min(1),
});

export const catalogToolSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().min(1),
  name: z.string().min(1),
  categories: z.array(toolCategorySchema).min(1),
  capabilities: z.array(z.string().min(1)).min(1),
  openness: opennessSchema,
  license: z.string().min(1),
  selfHost: z.enum(["yes", "no", "partial"]),
  cost: toolCostSchema,
  setupMode: setupModeSchema,
  effort: effortSchema,
  privacy: z.string().min(1),
  lockIn: z.string().min(1),
  prerequisites: z.array(z.string().min(1)),
  fallback: z.string().min(1),
  sources: z.array(z.object({
    label: z.string().min(1),
    url: z.string().url(),
  })).min(1),
  lastVerified: z.string().regex(/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/),
  status: toolStatusSchema,
  role: recommendationRoleSchema,
  harnessAlternative: z.boolean().default(false),
  challengeRelevance: z.string().min(1),
  notes: z.string().min(1),
  components: z.array(toolComponentSchema).default([]),

export type ToolCost = z.infer<typeof toolCostSchema>;

import { z } from "zod";

/**
 * Versioned tool catalog.
 *
 * Facts in this file are intentionally structured rather than embedded in
 * prose so that a recommendation can cite a source and a verification date.
 * Prices, quotas, and plan names change; the verification policy in
 * `docs/TOOL_CATALOG.md` defines when an entry must be re-checked.
 */
export const TOOL_CATALOG_VERSION = "2026.10.31.1";
export const TOOL_CATALOG_VERIFIED_ON = "2026-10-31";
export const TOOL_CATALOG_STALE_AFTER_DAYS = 120;

export const toolCategorySchema = z.enum([
  "web",
  "ai-inference",
  "fine-tuning",
  "tabular-data",
  "hardware",
  "voice",
  "browser-automation",
  "authentication",
  "search",
  "durable-workflows",
  "time-series-telemetry",
  "remote-database",
  "local-database",
  "vector-search",
  "public-deployment",
  "observability",
  "documentation",
  "ci",
  "code-history",
  "testing",
  "accessibility",
]);
export type ToolCategory = z.infer<typeof toolCategorySchema>;

export const opennessSchema = z.enum(["open-source", "open-weight", "proprietary", "mixed"]);
export type Openness = z.infer<typeof opennessSchema>;

export const costKindSchema = z.enum([
  "open-source",
  "open-weight",
  "self-hosted-free",
  "proprietary-free-tier",
  "trial",
  "paid-only",
  "hardware",
  "mixed",
]);
export type CostKind = z.infer<typeof costKindSchema>;

export const setupModeSchema = z.enum(["local", "hosted", "hybrid", "hardware"]);
export const effortSchema = z.enum(["low", "medium", "high"]);
export const toolStatusSchema = z.enum(["core", "conditional", "promo-only", "excluded"]);
export const recommendationRoleSchema = z.enum([
  "product-harness",
  "application",
  "observability",
  "build-history",
  "deployment",
  "utility",
]);

export const toolCostSchema = z.object({
  kind: costKindSchema,
  freeTier: z.boolean(),
  promotional: z.boolean(),
  permanentFree: z.boolean(),
  summary: z.string().min(1),
  limits: z.array(z.string().min(1)).min(1),
});

export const toolComponentSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1),
  openness: opennessSchema,
  license: z.string().min(1),
  costKind: costKindSchema,
  summary: z.string().min(1),
});

export const catalogToolSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().min(1),
  name: z.string().min(1),
  categories: z.array(toolCategorySchema).min(1),
  capabilities: z.array(z.string().min(1)).min(1),
  openness: opennessSchema,
  license: z.string().min(1),
  selfHost: z.enum(["yes", "no", "partial"]),
  cost: toolCostSchema,
  setupMode: setupModeSchema,
  effort: effortSchema,
  privacy: z.string().min(1),
  lockIn: z.string().min(1),
  prerequisites: z.array(z.string().min(1)),
  fallback: z.string().min(1),
  sources: z.array(z.object({
    label: z.string().min(1),
    url: z.string().url(),
  })).min(1),
  lastVerified: z.string().regex(/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/),
  status: toolStatusSchema,
  role: recommendationRoleSchema,
  harnessAlternative: z.boolean().default(false),
  challengeRelevance: z.string().min(1),
  notes: z.string().min(1),
  components: z.array(toolComponentSchema).default([]),
});

export type CatalogTool = z.infer<typeof catalogToolSchema>;
export type ToolCost = z.infer<typeof toolCostSchema>;

const verified = TOOL_CATALOG_VERIFIED_ON;

/**
 * The catalog is deliberately explicit about the difference between:
 * - open source (OSI-style software licence);
 * - open weights with a separate model licence;
 * - self-hosted free software;
 * - a proprietary free tier;
 * - trial or promotional credit;
 * - paid-only or hardware-dependent access.
 *
 * `status` is product policy, not a quality score:
 * - core: part of this product's baseline or its documented deployment mode;
 * - conditional: only when the idea and constraints fit;
 * - promo-only: never treated as permanent free usage;
 * - excluded: not a valid choice for this product.
 */
export const TOOL_CATALOG: CatalogTool[] = z.array(catalogToolSchema).parse([
  {
    id: "opencode",
    name: "OpenCode",
    categories: ["ai-inference", "code-history"],
    capabilities: ["Open-source coding harness", "Native sessions, tools, and permissions", "Model access through supported providers"],
    openness: "open-source",
    license: "MIT",
    selfHost: "yes",
    cost: {
      kind: "open-source",
      freeTier: true,
      promotional: false,
      permanentFree: true,
      summary: "Open-source harness. This workshop uses OpenCode's time-limited free DeepSeek route, not a permanent free-model guarantee.",
      limits: [
        "Model access and free offerings are provider terms and can change.",
        "This product does not bypass provider restrictions or substitute a paid fallback.",
      ],
    },
    setupMode: "local",

export const CATALOG_BY_ID = new Map(TOOL_CATALOG.map((tool) => [tool.id, tool]));

}

Now the engine. Need types for constraints and results. Let's write `src/server/recommendations/engine.ts`.

Need date difference robust. `daysBetween(from, to)`.

Idea text input: `idea` string composed from product proposal + open questions + sections maybe. Engine signature:
```
export interface RecommendationInput {
  idea: string;
  sections?: Array<{ id: string; title: string; content: string; status?: string }>;
  needs?: ToolCategory[] | null;
  constraints?: Partial<Constraints> | null;
  existingStack?: string[] | null;
  decisions?: ToolDecisionLike[];
  now?: Date | string;
  catalog?: CatalogTool[];
}
```
Catalog override for tests.

`Constraints`:
```
export interface RecommendationConstraints {
  noSpend: boolean;
  localOnly: boolean;
  openSourceOnly: boolean;
  privacySensitive: boolean;
  deadlineHours: number | null;
  hardwareAvailable: "none"|"arduino"|"unknown";
  existingStack: string[];
}
```
Partial explicit constraints in service stored.

Need `resolveConstraints` exported for tests.

`extractNeeds(text)` returns sorted ToolCategory[] in a stable order (enum order). Use keyword map.

Use `text.toLowerCase()`. Word boundary regex.

Need ensure "web" matches "website", "web app", "frontend", "browser app". Regex `/\b(web|website|web app|frontend|front-end|dashboard|react|html|css)\b/`.
Note `"lost-and-found"` idea may not include web. Fine.

`ai-inference`: `/\b(ai|llm|model|inference|assistant|chatbot|agent|machine learning|ml)\b/` — "AI" in "AI agents". Good.
But "email" contains "ai"? word boundary prevents.
`fine-tuning`: `/\b(fine[- ]?tun|train(ing)?|lora|rlhf|reinforcement learning|dataset)\b/`.
`tabular-data`: `/\b(tabular|csv|spreadsheet|table|prediction|predict|forecast|classification|regression|feature engineering)\b/`.
`hardware`: `/\b(arduino|sensor|hardware|iot|microcontroller|device|robot|circuit)\b/`.
`voice`: `/\b(voice|speech|audio|tts|text[- ]to[- ]speech|transcri|microphone|sound)\b/`.
`browser-automation`: `/\b(scrap(e|ing)|browser automation|automate (a )?browser|web automation|playwright|stagehand|headless browser|logged[- ]in)\b/`.
`authentication`: `/\b(auth|authentication|authorization|login|log[- ]in|sign[- ]in|oauth|user accounts?|identity|permissions?)\b/`.
`search`: `/\b(search|serp|google results|web results|find information|lookup)\b/` — "search" also vector search; okay.
`durable-workflows`: `/\b(workflow|durable|retry|retries|background job|long[- ]running|queue|orchestration|schedule(d)? task)\b/`.
`time-series-telemetry`: `/\b(time[- ]series|telemetry|metrics|monitor(ing)?|observability|trace(s|ing)?|logs?|sensor data)\b/`.
`remote-database`: `/\b(remote database|cloud database|managed database|postgres|mongodb|mysql|atlas|multi[- ]user|shared data)\b/`.
`local-database`: `/\b(sqlite|local database|embedded database|offline data|single[- ]file database)\b/`.
`vector-search`: `/\b(vector|embedding|semantic search|rag|similarity search)\b/`.
`public-deployment`: `/\b(deploy|deployment|hosted|public url|live site|production|share a link|domain)\b/`.
`observability`: `/\b(error tracking|sentry|observability|monitoring|instrumentation)\b/` overlaps telemetry.
`documentation`: `/\b(diagram|flowchart|architecture diagram|documentation|sequence diagram|mermaid)\b/`.
`ci`: `/\b(ci|continuous integration|github actions|pipeline|automated tests?)\b/`.
`code-history`: `/\b(session history|checkpoint|why (the )?code exists|agent history|entire)\b/`.
`testing`: `/\b(test|tests|testing|e2e|end[- ]to[- ]end|playwright|axe)\b/`.
`accessibility`: `/\b(accessib|wcag|a11y|screen reader|keyboard navigation|contrast)\b/`.

Need "web" tool recommendations: Which tools categories include "web"? None! We have no generic web framework tool. OpenCode? Render public-deployment, Playwright testing. The need `web` won't match any conditional tool except maybe none. That's a problem: recommendation for a web app should include SQLite, Playwright, axe, Render, Auth0 depending needs. `web` itself has no tool. That's okay; `web` is a need but no tool specifically. But tests "common idea profiles" for web app should get SQLite/Playwright/axe. The idea text includes "database" and "accessibility"/"test"? If not, only Render if "deploy". Could add a generic "web" category to Render? No. We could map `web` need to Playwright/axe/SQLite via fallback recommendations? Better: add a tool for "web" like `vite-react`? Not requested. The product itself uses React/Vite; but not in catalog. The prompt's requested tools don't include a web framework. It's fine if a web idea only gets baseline and maybe Render. But "recommendations change based on idea" tests can use different profiles.

Still, we should provide a recommendation for a web idea. Add categories "web" to Playwright? Playwright is testing, not web. Hmm. Could add a catalog entry for "Vite + React" but not requested and might bloat. The prompt says "Also include OpenCode, Ollama, SQLite, Playwright, axe-core, OpenTelemetry, Mermaid, and GitHub Actions where relevant." A web app should get Playwright/axe-core when testing/accessibility needs are present. The idea "campus lost-and-found web app with a search page and accessibility checks" triggers search, accessibility, testing -> Playwright, axe, SerpApi maybe (search intent), SQLite (local db? mention "database"). Good enough.

Need scoring to avoid recommending many tools for broad text. Limit 5.

`selectTop(candidates, 5)`. Baseline entries: opencode + entire (role product-harness/build-history), maybe always. Could include Sentry if not matched? Baseline should be OpenCode and Entire only. In the UI, show "Workshop baseline" with those two. Sentry only when matched. But "Core for this product: OpenCode, Entire, Sentry" - maybe baseline includes all 3. Let's include all 3 in baseline, and also allow Sentry in ranked if matched? Duplication. Better baseline includes all three, and exclude `role === "observability"` from ranked? Then Sentry never recommended to user's project. Hmm.

Let's define baseline as the product's own tools (OpenCode, Entire, Sentry, Render?) and not rank them, but rank other tools. The user's project recommendations are for their idea, while baseline is fixed. That meets "Core for this product". Sentry will be visible in baseline, so it's recommended for the product, but not for the user's app. The prompt says "Given an approved idea and constraints, the product recommends a small, ranked set of relevant tools" — the user's idea. Sentry could still be relevant. I think ranking Sentry when observability need is better. So baseline only OpenCode/Entire. Sentry is core policy but appears if relevant, with a core boost. We'll note in docs.

`baseline` result entries: build with `why` "Workshop baseline: ..." and `whyNot`. No add button? OpenCode/Entire are already selected, so `decision: "ADDED"`? Better `decision: "NONE"` but `canAddToPlan: false` and `existing: true`; UI shows "Baseline". Add `baseline: true` field. The result entries can have `alreadySelected: true`.

`existingStack` tools: if in existing stack, include in `alreadySelected`? We can set `existing: true`, score boost, and keep in recommendations with a "Already in your stack" flag, plus canAdd false? Actually adding an existing tool to plan is redundant. Set `canAddToPlan: false` when existing. But if the user mentions OpenCode, baseline already handles it.

Scoring and matching. Important: if constraints.openSourceOnly, `mixed` should be excluded? "open-source-only" means only open source. Mixed tools have proprietary components; safer to exclude mixed. But Stagehand is open source while Browserbase is proprietary; the combined entry is mixed. For openSourceOnly, exclude mixed to avoid recommending proprietary components. Tiger Data mixed includes open source TimescaleDB; excluding it may be too strict. Could allow mixed with a penalty if the specific component is open source. Simplicity: exclude `proprietary`; allow `mixed` with -8 and a `whyNot` warning "Mixed licensing: only part is open source." This is honest. Local-only: mixed may have hosted components; allow if selfHost yes/partial with penalty. For strong constraints, tests can check no `proprietary` entries.

NoSpend: `trial`/promo-only penalized but not excluded. `paid-only` excluded. `hardware` excluded? Arduino is hardware cost, so noSpend excludes it (`hardware` kind). That makes sense.

`localOnly`: exclude setupMode hosted if selfHost no; allow hybrid if selfHost yes/partial with penalty. Browserbase/Stagehand hybrid selfHost partial -> allowed (Stagehand local) with warning. Auth0 hosted no -> excluded. SerpApi hosted no -> excluded. GitHub Actions hosted, selfHost partial (self-hosted runners but control plane hosted) -> maybe exclude because selfHost partial? `localOnly` should not recommend hosted CI. We can exclude if setupMode === "hosted" && selfHost !== "yes". GitHub Actions selfHost "partial" -> exclude. Good.
`Render` hosted no -> excluded for localOnly.
`MongoDB Atlas` hosted partial -> excluded (Community Server escape hatch but managed). Good.
`Tiger Data` hybrid yes -> allowed with warning.

`privacySensitive`: hosted-only no self-host excluded? If privacy sensitive, exclude hosted no. Same as localOnly but less strict? Use -20 and keep? Better exclude to respect privacy. Tests can check.

`hardwareAvailable === "none"` excludes hardware category. If "arduino" allow.

Deadline: no exclusion, just score.

Need "conflicting tools": If SQLite and MongoDB both present, local/noSpend should rank SQLite higher. Add explicit conflict adjustment:
```
if (needs local-database && tool.id==="mongodb-atlas") score -= 4
if (constraints.localOnly && tool.id==="sqlite") score += 4
```
Not necessary; constraints already.

Maybe conflict between Playwright and Stagehand: if `needs` includes testing and browser-automation, Stagehand may rank high. Add `if tool.id==="browserbase-stagehand" && needs.includes("testing") && !needs.includes("browser-automation") score -= 6`; but categories include testing, so it would match. Better remove "testing" from browserbase-stagehand categories; it's browser automation, not a test runner. Use ["browser-automation"]. Then for a pure testing need, Playwright ranks. Good. Adjust catalog later.

Now result types. Let's write engine.

`Decision` type imported? Avoid circular: define `ToolDecision` in model.ts, import type. Engine can accept minimal shape:
```
export interface DecisionInput { toolId: string; status: "ADDED"|"DEFERRED"|"REJECTED"; decidedAt?: string; }
```

  tool: CatalogTool,

# Tool Catalog

Version: `2026.10.31.1`  
Last verified: `2026-10-31`  
Stale after: 120 days  
Source of truth: [`src/server/recommendations/catalog.ts`](../src/server/recommendations/catalog.ts)

The catalog is structured data, not a sponsor directory. Every entry carries a status, a licence/openness classification, a cost classification, material limits, official sources, and a last-verified date. The recommendation engine reads this data; it does not invent commercial facts from model prose.

## Classification policy

Use the narrowest true label. A tool can have components with different terms; those are recorded as `components` and summarised honestly rather than flattened into a misleading "free" claim.

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Open source** | Software is available under an OSI-style licence that permits inspection, modification, and self-hosting within its terms. |
| **Open weight** | Model weights are downloadable, but a separate model licence governs use, redistribution, or production. Open weight is **not** the same as open source. |
| **Self-hosted free software** | The software can run on infrastructure you control without a service fee; hardware and operations are still costs. |
| **Proprietary free tier** | A commercial service offers a free plan with quotas and terms that can change. Free tier does not mean unlimited or permanent. |
| **Trial or promotional credit** | Time-limited, account-limited, or event-limited value. It is never counted as permanent free usage. |
| **Paid-only** | Use requires payment. A credit, if any, is not a free tier. |
| **Hardware-dependent** | The software may be open, but a physical device, components, shipping, or delivery time is required. |

`$0` new cash spending is the product's default. A recommendation may mention a paid tool only with an explicit warning and a fallback; adding it to the plan never authorises spending.

## Status policy

`status` is product policy, not a quality score.

- **core** — part of this product's baseline or its documented deployment mode. OpenCode, Entire, Sentry, and Render (only under the documented mode/cost constraints).
- **conditional** — appropriate only when the idea and constraints fit. This includes strong local/open choices such as Ollama, SQLite, Playwright, axe-core, OpenTelemetry, Mermaid, Temporal, and the open Tiger Data components.
- **promo-only** — value is promotional or trial-based rather than default-free: Tinker, DigitalOcean, Backboard, Ultramarine, and the `.tech` domain.
- **excluded** — not a valid product harness choice: GitHub Copilot.

A higher status does not guarantee a recommendation. A tool must match a real need and survive the active constraints. Challenge sponsorship never adds score.

## Catalog

| Tool | Status | Openness / licence | Cost classification | Self-host | Setup / effort | Verified |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | core | Open source, MIT | Open source; free-model route is time-limited | Yes | Local / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Entire | core | Mixed: MIT CLI, hosted platform | Mixed: free local CLI, separate hosted service | Partial | Local / low | 2026-10-31 |
| Sentry Agent Tracing | core | Proprietary service; open SDKs | Proprietary free tier with quotas | Partial | Hybrid / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Render | core (documented constraints) | Proprietary service | Proprietary free tier; persistent disk and always-on compute are paid | No | Hosted / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Gemma | conditional | Open weight with a separate model licence | Open weights; hardware or host required | Yes | Local / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Ollama | conditional | Open source, MIT | Open source, permanent free | Yes | Local / low | 2026-10-31 |
| SQLite | conditional | Open source, public domain | Open source, permanent free | Yes | Local / low | 2026-10-31 |
| Playwright | conditional | Open source, Apache-2.0 | Open source, permanent free | Yes | Local / low | 2026-10-31 |
| axe-core | conditional | Open source, MPL-2.0 | Open source, permanent free | Yes | Local / low | 2026-10-31 |
| OpenTelemetry | conditional | Open source, Apache-2.0 | Open source, permanent free | Yes | Local / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Mermaid | conditional | Open source, MIT | Open source, permanent free | Yes | Local / low | 2026-10-31 |
| GitHub Actions | conditional | Proprietary service; user-owned workflow files | Proprietary free minutes, then paid | Partial | Hosted / low | 2026-10-31 |
| TabPFN | conditional | Open weight; code Apache-2.0, model weights non-commercial | Mixed: free evaluation/non-commercial, commercial licence for production | Yes | Local / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Tinker | promo-only | Proprietary service | Trial/promotional credit; usage-based training | No | Hosted / high | 2026-10-31 |
| Arduino | conditional | Open-source software and hardware designs | Hardware-dependent; boards and components cost money | Yes | Hardware / high | 2026-10-31 |
| DigitalOcean | promo-only | Proprietary service | Trial/promotional new-account credit, then paid | No | Hosted / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Auth0 for AI Agents | conditional | Proprietary service | Proprietary free tier; paid production plans | No | Hosted / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Backboard | promo-only | Proprietary service; R-CLI marketed as open source | Promotional/hackathon credit; balance unconfirmed | No | Hosted / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| ElevenLabs | conditional | Proprietary service | Proprietary free tier with monthly quota; paid plans | No | Hosted / low | 2026-10-31 |
| Browserbase / Stagehand | conditional | Mixed: Stagehand Apache-2.0, Browserbase proprietary | Mixed: open SDK, hosted browser sessions metered | Partial | Hybrid / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| GitHub Copilot | excluded | Proprietary service | Separate commercial subscription/free tier | No | Hosted / low | 2026-10-31 |
| Mastra | conditional | Mixed: Apache-2.0 core, enterprise source-available | Open-source core; enterprise features separate | Yes | Local / high | 2026-10-31 |
| MongoDB Atlas | conditional | Proprietary managed service; Community Server uses SSPL | Proprietary free tier (M0, 512 MB) then paid | Partial | Hosted / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| Ultramarine 1 Flash | promo-only | Open weight; hosted API paid | Trial/promotional credit, not permanent free | Yes | Hybrid / medium | 2026-10-31 |
| SerpApi | conditional | Proprietary service | Proprietary free tier (limited monthly searches) then paid | No | Hosted / low | 2026-10-31 |
| `.tech` domain | promo-only | Proprietary registration service | Paid registration; any free/discount offer is promotional | No | Hosted / low | 2026-10-31 |
| Temporal | conditional | Open source, MIT server | Self-hosted free; Temporal Cloud is paid with trial credit | Yes | Local / high | 2026-10-31 |
| Tiger Data | conditional | Mixed: open-source TimescaleDB components, proprietary Tiger Cloud | Mixed: self-host free components; Tiger Cloud 30-day trial then paid | Yes | Hybrid / medium | 2026-10-31 |

## Sources and material limits

These are the official sources used for the 2026-10-31 verification. Re-check them before changing a classification or repeating a quota claim.

| Tool | Official sources | Material limits recorded in the catalog |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | [docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/) · [source](https://github.com/sst/opencode) | Provider model access and free offerings can change; this product does not bypass restrictions or use a paid fallback. |
| Entire | [docs](https://docs.entire.com/) · [CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli) | Local capture may contain prompts, paths, and tool calls; sanitize before sharing. Hosted collaboration is separate. |
| Sentry Agent Tracing | [agent tracing](https://docs.sentry.io/product/agents/getting-started/) · [pricing](https://sentry.io/pricing/) | Event quotas, retention, and plan features vary; account access is unverified until a trace is received. |
| Render | [pricing](https://render.com/pricing) · [free plan](https://render.com/docs/free) | Free web services sleep; persistent disks and always-on services are paid. The hosted workshop needs a disk. |
| Gemma | [models](https://deepmind.google/models/gemma/) · [terms](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/terms) | The specific release's model card and licence govern use; local inference needs hardware. |
| Ollama | [site](https://ollama.com/) · [source](https://github.com/ollama/ollama) | Local models need disk, memory, and compute; each model keeps its own licence. |
| SQLite | [site](https://sqlite.org/) · [copyright](https://sqlite.org/copyright.html) | Single-writer/local-disk assumptions; not a distributed multi-user database. |
| Playwright | [site](https://playwright.dev/) · [source](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright) | Managed browser grids are separate; flaky or authenticated flows need test design. |
| axe-core | [source](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) · [Deque](https://www.deque.com/axe/) | Automated rules cover only a subset; manual keyboard, focus, and contrast checks remain necessary. |
| OpenTelemetry | [site](https://opentelemetry.io/) · [source](https://github.com/open-telemetry) | A backend/exporter is still required; telemetry needs redaction. |
| Mermaid | [site](https://mermaid.js.org/) · [source](https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid) | Layout may need tuning; a diagram does not verify implementation. |
| GitHub Actions | [docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions) · [billing](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/managing-billing-for-github-actions/about-billing-for-github-actions) | Private-repository minutes/storage are quota-limited; hosted runners are not local-only. |
| TabPFN | [models and licences](https://docs.priorlabs.ai/models) · [Prior Labs](https://priorlabs.ai/) | Weights are non-commercial for current releases; production/commercial use needs a licence or API agreement. |
| Tinker | [Tinker](https://thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/) · [pricing](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/models/#pricing-terms) | Training, sampling, and checkpoint storage are metered; a small credit is promotional. |
| Arduino | [site](https://www.arduino.cc/) · [software](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software) | Boards, sensors, shipping, and delivery time are real costs; no hardware means no build. |
| DigitalOcean | [pricing](https://www.digitalocean.com/pricing) · [signup credit](https://docs.digitalocean.com/platform/billing/signup-credit/) | New-account credit expires and requires a payment method; resources bill after credit. |
| Auth0 for AI Agents | [AI](https://auth0.com/ai) · [pricing](https://auth0.com/pricing) | Free developer tier has MAU/feature limits; production generally needs a paid plan. |
| Backboard | [hackathon](https://backboard.io/hackathon) · [site](https://backboard.io/) | Hackathon access/credits are promotional; balance, limits, and continuation pricing are not assumed. |
| ElevenLabs | [pricing](https://elevenlabs.io/pricing) · [docs](https://elevenlabs.io/docs) | Monthly character/credit quota; voice cloning and commercial use have extra terms. |
| Browserbase / Stagehand | [Stagehand](https://stagehand.dev/) · [Browserbase pricing](https://www.browserbase.com/pricing) · [source](https://github.com/browserbase/stagehand) | Hosted browser minutes and concurrency are metered; hosted sessions see page content and credentials. |
| GitHub Copilot | [product](https://github.com/features/copilot) · [docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot) | Excluded as a runtime harness. A separate subscription/free tier does not change that policy. |
| Mastra | [site](https://mastra.ai/) · [source](https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra) | Enterprise features are source-available, not OSI open source; a framework adds dependencies and model-routing choices. |
| MongoDB Atlas | [pricing](https://www.mongodb.com/pricing) · [free-tier limits](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/) | M0 has 512 MB shared storage and limited operations; backups and some features are restricted. |

# Product Brief

**Unfinished Business — Bring your ideas to life.**

## User value

A first-time hackathon builder has an approved idea but not a clear stack. They are surrounded by generous-sounding tools, trial credits, and sponsor pages, and cannot tell which choices are actually open, free, local, compatible, or worth the setup time.

The Phase 5 recommendation engine turns the approved idea and the builder's constraints into a small, ranked, inspectable set of tools. It explains:

- **Why** a tool fits the idea.
- **Why not** it might be a poor choice.
- **What it needs** before it can be used.
- **How much effort** it likely adds.
- **What limits** apply, including licence, cost, quota, privacy, and lock-in.
- **What to use instead** if it does not fit.

The result is a planning aid, not an installation wizard or a sponsor directory.

## Who it is for

- A beginner or AI-assisted builder who needs a defensible next choice.
- A builder with explicit constraints: no spending, local-only, open-source-only, privacy-sensitive data, a short deadline, limited hardware, or an existing stack.
- A user who wants to understand the tradeoff instead of accepting a model's confident tool list.

## What changes in the journey

1. The Oracle clarifies and the user approves the idea.
2. The Architect drafts one section at a time. The **Tools, access, and cost** section is the natural home for the recommendation panel.
3. The panel extracts or accepts needs such as web, AI inference, fine-tuning, tabular data, hardware, voice, browser automation, authentication, search, durable workflows, time-series/telemetry, remote or local data, vector search, and public deployment.
4. The user filters by constraints and reviews a ranked set of at most five tools.
5. The user adds, defers, or rejects a recommendation.
6. **Adding requires the Tools section to be approved.** The decision is stored with the catalog version and verification date.
7. The Witness and export views show selected tools as planning notes, separate from approved plan sections.

## Recommendation boundaries

The product must not:

- install a tool, run an installer, or change the user's machine;
- create an account, accept terms, or claim a promotional credit;
- deploy, publish, or submit anything;
- authorize spending or a paid overage;
- recommend a tool only because it sponsors a challenge;
- treat trial credit as permanent free usage;
- present a model-generated cost, quota, licence, or compatibility claim as fact;
- recommend a harness switch away from OpenCode;
- recommend Mastra or Backboard for the workshop's own internal orchestration;
- claim a challenge category without implemented usage and evidence.

The product may:

- show official source links and a last-verified date;
- say that a fact is stale and needs re-checking;
- say that a tool is a poor fit for the current constraints;
- show a fallback that keeps the project moving;
- preserve an explicit rejection or deferral so the user is not asked again in the same session.

## User-visible states

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Recommended | Matched the idea and survived the current constraints. |
| Added | The user approved adding it to the plan. Nothing was installed or authorized. |
| Deferred | The user wants to revisit it later. |
| Rejected | The user does not want it recommended again for this project. |
| Stale | The catalog fact is past the 120-day verification window. |
| Blocked | A constraint excludes it, or the Tools section is not approved yet. |

## Success criteria

- Recommendations change when the idea changes.
- Recommendations change when constraints change.
- Promotional tools never rank as default-free.
- A local-only or no-spend project is not told to use a hosted paid service as its first choice.
- An OpenCode-only project is never advised to switch harnesses.
- The user can explain why a tool was suggested and what it would cost in effort and commitments.
- Every addition is an explicit, reversible-in-planning decision with no external effect.

## Non-goals

Phase 5 does not add a marketplace, automatic installation, account provisioning, credit claiming, price comparison, live quota checks, model-generated fact lookup, or challenge submission. Phase 6 is not started.

- Promotional tools never rank as default-free.
- A local-only or no-spend project is not told to use a hosted paid service as its first choice.
- An OpenCode-only project is never advised to switch harnesses.
- The user can explain why a tool was suggested and what it would cost in effort and commitments.
- Every addition is an explicit, reversible-in-planning decision with no external effect.

## Non-goals

Phase 5 does not add a marketplace, automatic installation, account provisioning, credit claiming, price comparison, live quota checks, model-generated fact lookup, or challenge submission. Phase 6 is not started.

# UX and Visual System

The recommendation panel extends the existing haunted-workshop visual system. It is a working document, not a storefront: readable cards, explicit caveats, and a visible approval gate.

## Existing visual tokens

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--bg` | `#111018` | Page background |
| `--surface` | `#1B1824` | Panels and document |
| `--raised` | `#252031` | Cards, badges, secondary actions |
| `--text` | `#F4F0E8` | Primary copy |
| `--muted` | `#B8AFCA` | Metadata and supporting copy |
| `--accent` | `#F4B66C` | Primary action, headings, source links |
| `--spirit` | `#BFA3FF` | Stage accents, focused/selected state |
| `--success` | `#8BD5A7` | Positive fit, approved seal |
| `--danger` | `#FFB4A8` | Errors and stale-data warnings |
| Spacing | 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24 / 32 px | All layout spacing |

Typography remains system sans for work text, restrained serif for headings, and monospace for evidence/metadata. Cards never rely on color alone; each state has a text label.

## Placement

The full recommendation panel appears inside the **Tools, access, and cost** section of the Architect stage. This keeps it next to the section it informs and prevents it from bypassing section review.

A compact **Tools** summary appears in the right-hand activity column after the product is approved. It shows:

- selected count and ranked count;
- catalog version and verification date;
- a stale-data warning when applicable;
- selected tool names and cost classifications.

The Witness stage shows **Selected tools** as read-only planning notes. The export includes `selectedTools` separately from the approved plan.

## Panel anatomy

1. **Eyebrow and heading** — `TOOLS & BUDGET`, `Idea-aware recommendations`.
2. **Catalog line** — version, verification date, staleness window.
3. **Warning stack** — stale catalog, no-spend reminder, local-only/open-source-only notices.
4. **Filters** — detected needs chips, focus-need select, constraint checkboxes, deadline hours, hardware availability, `Apply filters`.
5. **Boundary note** — deterministic rules and the no-install/no-account/no-spend statement.
6. **Gate banner** — shown until the Tools section is approved.
7. **Recommendation grid** — at most five cards, one column on narrow screens.
8. **Baseline disclosure** — OpenCode and Entire, explicitly not ranked against alternatives.
9. **Added to the plan** — selected tools with licence/cost summary and verification date.
10. **Decisions** — ADDED/DEFERRED/REJECTED history.

## Recommendation card

```text
TOOLS & BUDGET
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ conditional · open-source · low effort      │
│ SQLite                                #1    │
│ Embedded relational database · …            │
│ Fit: Public-domain embedded database …      │
│ ✓ Matches the local database need …         │
│ ✓ Open source under Public domain …         │
│ ✓ Has a permanent free/open path …          │
│ ▸ Why not, prerequisites, and limits        │
│ Fallback: Use JSON files for a tiny demo …  │
│ Privacy: … Lock-in: …                       │
│ Verified 2026-10-31. Sources: …             │
│ [Add to plan] [Defer] [Reject]              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Card content rules

- **Name and rank** are always visible.
- **Status, openness, effort, setup** appear as a compact metadata line.
- **Fit** uses the catalog cost summary, not a model-generated claim.
- **Why** is a short list of positive, evidence-backed reasons.
- **Why not, prerequisites, and limits** are in a disclosure so the card stays scannable without hiding the tradeoffs.
- **Fallback** is always present.
- **Privacy and lock-in** are always shown.
- **Sources and verification date** are linked.
- **Challenge relevance** is shown as a sentence and never as a badge that implies a win.
- **Actions** are explicit and never look like an install button.

## States

| State | Visual treatment | Copy |
|---|---|---|
| Recommended | Raised card, rank badge | `#1` … `#5` |
| Added | Spirit-colored border, `ADDED` badge | “Added to the plan” |
| Deferred | `DEFERRED` badge | “Revisit later” |
| Rejected | `REJECTED` badge; removed from ranked cards | “Not for this project” |
| Stale | Danger-colored `stale data` badge and banner | “Re-check the linked official sources…” |
| Gate closed | Add button disabled; banner explains why | “Approve the Tools, access, and cost section before adding…” |
| Empty result | Calm banner | “No tool matched this combination…” |
| Loading | Status banner | “Reading the approved idea for tool needs…” |
| Error | Danger banner, retry guidance | “Tool recommendations could not be loaded…” |

## Filters

- **Detected needs** are read-only chips from deterministic extraction.
- **Focus a need** sends an explicit need override. `All detected needs` sends `null` and restores extraction.
- **No spending** defaults on because the product's cash cap is `$0`.
- **Local only** excludes hosted-only tools and down-ranks hybrid tools.
- **Open source only** excludes proprietary tools and down-ranks mixed licences with a visible warning.
- **Privacy-sensitive** excludes hosted-only tools and surfaces data-handling notes.
- **Deadline hours** reduces the rank of high-effort tools at 24 hours or less.
- **Hardware** can be `Unknown`, `None available`, or `Arduino available`; `None` excludes hardware-dependent tools.
- **Existing stack** is carried from the project context; matching tools are marked and not presented as a switch.

Applying filters persists them in `recommendationContext` and returns a fresh recommendation result. Filters never change an approved section.

## Warnings and boundaries

- The catalog warning is non-dismissible while stale data exists.
- Promotional tools always show a “temporary, not permanent free” reason.
- The plan-gate banner is shown until the Tools section is approved.
- The boundary note is repeated at the panel and on each card's limitations.
- No card uses the words “free forever”, “unlimited”, or a price that is not in the catalog.
- A challenge sponsor never receives a special visual treatment.

## Accessibility

- Semantic headings (`h2`, `h3`), `fieldset`/`legend`, labels, and lists.
- Native checkboxes, selects, and number inputs; no custom widgets that lose keyboard behavior.
- Focus ring uses a solid outline plus `box-shadow` for headless/browser compatibility.
- Cards reflow to one column at narrow widths; long tool names and source URLs wrap.
- Stale and error states use text, not color alone.
- The panel respects the existing reduced-motion policy; it introduces no ambient animation.
- Source links open in a new tab with `rel="noreferrer"` and visible labels.

## Responsive layout

- Below 600 px: filters and cards stack in one column; action buttons wrap.
- 600–959 px: filters use two columns; cards auto-fit.
- 960 px and above: the existing three-column frame remains; the recommendation panel stays in the central reading column.

## Copy guidelines

- Prefer “recommendation”, “planning decision”, and “fit” over “deal”, “offer”, or “must use”.
- Say “promotional credit”, never “free”.
- Say “open weights”, never “open source” for a model with a separate licence.
- Say “adding records a plan decision” and list what it does not do.
- Say “No challenge claim without implemented usage and evidence.”
- Keep the fallback concrete and local.
